extracted.intended_audience: students and philosophers studying logic; instructors of logic
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for forming and testing definitions (names, connotation/denotation) and for judging legitimate inference (conversion, induction, ratiocination) in formal logic and philosophy of language. Focuses on what makes a good definition, how language grows and should be mended, and what counts as genuine reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions are of names, not of things
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions are properly of names only, and not of things; assertions respecting the meaning of words (definitions) are not susceptible of truth or falsity, nor therefore of proof or disproof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat definitions as stipulations about connotation/denotation of terms rather than factual claims. When evaluating a definition, distinguish whether the issue is a matter of usage/meaning (verbal) or of fact (real/propositional).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions tacitly postulate existence of connoted attributes/ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a definition refers to an ideal or mental object not occurring in nature, the definition postulates the real existence of the idea or of the attributes it connotes (e.g., definition of a geometrical line postulates the notion of length without breadth, or more soundly, length as an attribute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing definitions used in demonstrative reasoning, check what factual or mental postulates are implicitly assumed by the definition—proofs rest upon those postulates rather than on words alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining an abstract name is often difficult and may require deep inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: How to define a name may turn upon considerations going deep into the nature of the things which are denoted by the name (examples: 'What is rhetoric?', 'What is justice?', 'What is virtue?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect definitional tasks for abstract/general terms to demand empirical, historical, or substantive philosophical investigation rather than mere citation of conventional meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find a meaning compatible with continued denotation
rubrics_metrics.description: When inquiring into the definition of the name of any real object, one tacitly assumes that a meaning must be found compatible with its continuing to denote, if possible all, but at any rate the greater or the more important part, of the things of which it is commonly predicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer definitions that preserve ordinary usage where feasible; evaluate candidate definitions by how well they retain the term's application to the important/majority cases rather than discarding established denotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative stages for defining a general/abstract name
rubrics_metrics.description: To define a general name investigate: (1) whether mankind agree as to what is called by the name (usage/convention); (2) whether the actions/things form a class at all (a matter of fact); (3) if they do, what common quality they possess; (4) if not, how best to form an artificial class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this sequence when evaluating or forming a definition: check usage, check empirical unity of class, identify common attributes, and if necessary propose an artificial classificatory scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select connoted attributes of greatest importance (differentia → interesting propria)
rubrics_metrics.description: In giving a distinct connotation the philosopher will endeavour to fix upon such attributes as, while they are common to all the things usually denoted by the name, are also of greatest importance in themselves ... He will select, as far as possible, such differentia as lead to the greatest number of interesting propria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing distinguishing features for a definition, prefer attributes that are widely shared among the denoted class and that produce many significant consequences (propria) rather than obscure or recondite qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a name's denotation has become confused, restrict and mend it
rubrics_metrics.description: When a name becomes applied to a confused huddle of objects (connotes nothing even vague), it has become unfit for thought/communication; it must be stripped of some part of its multifarious denotation and confined to objects possessed of some attributes in common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate and reform terms that are overly ambiguous by narrowing their denotation to a coherent subclass sharing definite attributes to restore the term's utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the spontaneous growth of language before remodeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The study of the spontaneous growth of languages is of the utmost importance to the philosopher who would logically remodel them; established groupings, though rude, often contain materials well suited for logical retouching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When revising terminology, consult the history and customary usage of terms: existing classifications often capture practical distinctions and should inform any logical redefinition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish apparent (equipollent) inference from real inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where the conclusion is merely a repetition, or part, of the assertion contained in the premiss (equipollency/conversion that repeats content) are not real inferences. Examples include rephrasings, inferring particulars from universals by mere wording, or affirming something already connoted by antecedent predicates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge an argument as a genuine inference only if the conclusion asserts something not already contained in the premisses; beware of treating rewordings or implicit restatements as proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for legitimate conversion and limits of conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Legitimate conversions: Some A is B → Some B is A; No A is B → No B is A. From All A is B you cannot infer All B is A, but you may infer Some B is A (conversion per accidens). From Some A is not B you cannot infer Some B is not A; legitimate transformation may require contraposition or alteration of terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating arguments that convert subject and predicate, apply these conversion rules and identify invalid conversions (illicit generalisation, improper inference of existence). Use contraposition only when terms are properly altered as the text describes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify propositions by what they assert (subject/attribute analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever its form, the real subject of every proposition is some fact(s) or phenomenon(s) of consciousness or hidden causes; what is predicated is always one of: Existence, Order in Place, Order in Time, Causation, or Resemblance. In common terms: propositions assert that a subject does or does not possess some attribute, or that attributes are or are not conjoined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification to analyze propositions before attempting proof: determine whether the claim concerns existence, order, causation or resemblance, and frame appropriate evidence or inference methods accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Induction and Ratiocination (syllogism) by generality of conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction: inferring a proposition from propositions less general than itself (conclusion more general than premisses). Ratiocination (syllogism): inferring a proposition from propositions equally or more general (conclusion less general or equally general).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose induction when aiming to generalize from particular instances; use ratiocination/syllogistic reasoning when deductively deriving particulars from general premises. Evaluate whether the conclusion's generality exceeds that of antecedents to determine whether inductive warrant is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive conclusions go beyond their premises (generalisation requires evidential warrant)
rubrics_metrics.description: A principle ascertained by experience is more than a mere summing up of what was specifically observed; it is a generalisation grounded on cases and expressive of belief that what was found true is true in an indefinite number of unobserved cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising inductive arguments, demand appropriate evidential basis and consider whether the sample/cases justify generalising beyond observed instances; recognise induction adds substantive content needing support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate skill in recognising identity of assertions under diverse wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Although conversion that merely reasserts is not inference, an important intellectual habit is discerning rapidly and surely the identity of an assertion when disguised under diversity of language; rules of opposition and technical logical language serve this purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train to detect when two differently worded propositions are equivalent or merely formatter variants; this skill is essential for clear reasoning and for avoiding fallacies that hinge on superficial paraphrase differences.
